newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE - Peru and rebels go underground - to tunnels.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Peru and rebels go underground - to tunnels.

text.p: First, leftist rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) accused Peru's government of digging a secret tunnel under the besieged Japanese ambassador's home to rescue the 72 hostages inside.
Then, police found a tunnel built by teenage members of the MRTA in a youth prison, through which they planned to escape from jail.
Two days later, people living near a women's detention centre where several MRTA guerrillas were also being held heard strange noises under the street.
Their conclusion? Another tunnel.

Tunnels have a long and hallowed -- make that hollowed -- place in Peruvian history, and now they have become the latest and weirdest tactic in the struggle of wills between President Alberto Fujimori's government and the Marxist guerrilla group.
"Are we a nation of moles?" asked a headline in the Lima newspaper La Republica in reporting on all the excavating.

News reports have spoken of as many as four tunnels being dug out beneath the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence, while police have been tapping and poking the ground at jails around the country in search of any more undiscovered shafts.
In a country where the economy depends on mining, it should come as no surprise that so many people know how to dig long, safe underground shafts.
"Any mine worker is able to build this sort of project without the need for much instruction," said Alfonso Priale, a civil engineer, referring to the recently found MRTA tunnel.
A GRAND PERUVIAN UNDERGROUND TRADITION
"Whoever made it probably knew how to do it by tradition. There are many, many people in Peru who know how to build tunnels," he said on local television.

The tunnel as tactic in MRTA's war to overthrow the Peruvian state goes back to 1990, when 48 members of the group, including its leader Victor Polay, fled from the maximum security Canto Grande jail through a secret tunnel.
Polay was recaptured in 1992 but the daring 1990 tunnel escape remained MRTA's finest moment -- until last Dec. 17.

That evening, a band of about 20 MRTA fighters blasted a hole in an outer wall and swarmed into the Japanese residence during a cocktail party and took all 500 guests hostage, including much of the cream of Peruvian society. They later released all but 72 of them.
Yet the tunnel still represents "the emblem of the greatest public relations coups (MRTA) has achieved both inside and outside the country," said the news magazine Caretas.

"If someone conducted a poll of the members of MRTA as to what their favourite book is, the chosen work would without a doubt be Ernesto Sabato's 'The Tunnel,'" said Caretas. The police's efforts to take back the residence via their own tunnels might be an attempt at ironic revenge for the 1990 episode, the magazine said.
MRTA includes in its ranks many experienced excavators, according to an absorbing, blow-by-blow account of the 1990 jailbreak just published in the United States, entitled "Tunnel to Canto Grande."
The tunnel took three years to build and stretched for about 300 yards (metres) from a safehouse into the prison, where MRTA inmates wheedled, cajoled and bribed their way past guards, says the book.
TUNNEL WITH STYLE

No mere hole in the ground, the MRTA tunnel had stuccoed ceilings, cement floors, timber supports, electric lighting and even a small library where diggers could unwind with tracts on Marxist political economy during their rest hours.

"I was always happy to go down in the tunnel ... It's a bit gloomy, dark and damp, but it has a certain charm. There's nothing more amazing than total darkness," the book quotes one of the rebels as recalling.
Tunnels have long been a part of Peruvian history. Downtown Lima is honeycombed with catacombs, crypts and underground passageways built over two centuries as public burial grounds.

The maze of tunnels, built starting in the 17th century and until the early 1800s, contain the bones and skulls of thousands of Peruvians, all neatly arranged at the bottom of dusty crypts. They are still a ghoulish tourist attraction.

"Almost every house in the centre of Lima has at least one tunnel underneath it. It's possible there are still some unexplored tunnels down there," said Father Anselmo Diaz of San Francisco church, which offers tours of the maze of tunnels beneath its floor. Claustrophobics abstain.

Peruvians buried their dead in tunnels in Spanish colonial times because ground-level burials were thought to spread disease. In this century, leftist activists used tunnels as hideouts during political persecution in the 1930s.
